summary: Josef Kuckertz worked in Indology and ethnomusicology. Educated at the Rheinische Musikschule and the University of Cologne (Ph.D. c. 1962, habilitation c. 1967), he held posts at Cologne (Professor from 1970), Göttingen (1978–1980), and the Free University of Berlin (Professor, 1980).

Josef Maria Abs worked in Indology and philosophy. He studied at the University of Bonn (c. 1913–1921) under Hermann Jacobi (c. 1913–1920) and held a professorship at the University of Calcutta in 1914.

Josef Markwart was a scholar of Iranian and Central Asian studies, history, and linguistics. He studied at Tübingen (Ph.D. c. 1893) and Bonn, then held posts at Tübingen, Leiden, the National Museum of Ethnology (1900–1912), and Berlin (from 1912).

Josef Partsch was a historian and archaeologist who studied at the University of Breslau (c. 1900–1905). He held appointments in Berlin (c. 1905–1908), Geneva (c. 1907–1908), Göttingen (c. 1908–1912), Freiburg (c. 1912–1920), and Bonn (c. 1920–1925).

Linguist Josef Schick studied at Tübingen under Albrecht Weber (c. 1878–1882) and earned his PhD at Humboldt University of Berlin (1889). He held positions in Berlin, Bonn, and Heidelberg before serving as professor at Munich (1896–1925).

Art historian Josef Strzygowski studied in Vienna, Berlin, and Munich (Ph.D. c. 1885). He held academic posts at the University of Vienna (1887, and professor 1909–1933), the University of Graz (1892), and Åbo Akademi University (1921–1925).

Indologist and linguist Josef Zubatý studied under Alfred Ludwig at Charles University (Ph.D. c. 1883). He spent his career at Charles University, serving as Privatdozent from 1885 and Professor of Sanskrit and comparative Indo-European from 1894 to 1925.
Josef van Ess was a scholar of religious studies. He completed his studies at the University of Bonn (c. 1954–1959) and held a post at the University of Tübingen from c. 1968 to 1999.
Indologist Joseph Ammann studied under Othmar Frank and worked as a teacher at the Hans-Carossa-Gymnasium Landshut in 1836.

Religious studies scholar Joseph Campbell studied at Canterbury School, Dartmouth, Columbia (B.A. 1925, master's c. 1927), Paris, and Munich. He was a research fellow at Columbia (1927) and taught at Canterbury School (1933) and Sarah Lawrence College (1934–1972).
Joseph D. Markowski is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Japanology who earned a Master of Arts at McGill University under the supervision of G. Victor Sōgen Hori (attested 2004).

Indologist Joseph Dahlmann studied at Stella Matutina, Vienna under Georg Bühler, and Berlin (Ph.D. 1900). A founder of Sophia University, he taught there in 1913 and served at the University of Tokyo from 1914 to 1924.

Joseph Dalton Hooker earned an M.D. from the University of Glasgow (c. 1839). He served at the British Geological Survey (1845–1847) and later worked at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, as Assistant Director and Director (1855–1885).

Joseph David Beglar worked in archaeology and Indology after studying at Hooghly Mohsin College and IIEST Shibpur. He served in the Bengal Public Works Department (1864) and the Archaeological Survey of India (from 1871; Archaeological Surveyor of Bengal 1885–1890).

Indologist and historical geographer Joseph E. Schwartzberg studied at Brooklyn College, Maryland, the Sorbonne, and Wisconsin-Madison (PhD 1960 under Richard Hartshorne). He served at Penn, Jawaharlal Nehru University, and was long-term geography professor at the University of Minnesota (1964–2000).

Classicist Joseph Edward Harry studied at Johns Hopkins University under Maurice Bloomfield. He held posts as professor at Georgetown College (1888–1900) and the University of Cincinnati (1900–1916), lecturer at the Sorbonne (1919–1922), and faculty member at Bard College (1926–1939).

Linguist and Indologist Joseph Edward Lyall Brandreth was educated at Eton College (c. 1836–1840) and the East India Company College (c. 1840–1842). He later served as a member of the Imperial Legislative Council from 1867 to 1869.

Joseph Estlin Carpenter studied at University College London, the University of London, Harris Manchester College, and Zurich. He was Wilde Lecturer at Oxford (1914–1924) and held multiple roles at Harris Manchester College, including professor, president, and principal.

Joseph Gabet was a scholar of Tibetology, Sinology, and religious studies who was educated at the Petit Séminaire de Vaux-sur-Poligny (c. 1823–1828) and the Grand Séminaire de Saint-Claude (c. 1828–1833).

Buddhist studies and religious figure Joseph Goldstein studied at Columbia University and under numerous Buddhist masters. He co-founded the Insight Meditation Society (1974) and Barre Center for Buddhist Studies (1989), and taught at Naropa University in 1974.
